episodes.210813: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
episodes.210814: On April 3rd, severe thunderstorms swept through the central Indiana region, with Warren County specifically targeted by an isolated stronger storm that tracked across the county, producing 1 inch hail near the Tippecanoe County border. The hail was part of a broader severe system that also triggered tornado warnings in adjacent Benton County.
episodes.211371: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northern Illinois during the evening of April 2nd producing wind damage and three tornadoes.
episodes.211372: Scattered thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the evening of April 2nd.
episodes.211763: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. Later in the evening, an intense complex of thunderstorms moved from west-central into east-central Oklahoma, including across the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area. This cluster produced swaths of damaging winds and several tornadoes. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
episodes.211854: A low pressure system tracked across southeast Iowa during the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026. Temperatures across central Illinois pushed into the 70s, with dewpoints in the low 60s, and the environment featured moderate instability and wind shear. Scattered supercells developed and produced four tornadoes, hail up to the size of ping pong balls, and damaging winds, primarily near and northwest of the Illinois River Valley. All of the tornadoes were rated EF-0 or EF-1, and no injuries were reported.
episodes.211855: A warm front gradually lifted north across central Illinois during the afternoon and evening on April 3rd, 2026. The environment south of the front featured robust moisture, strong instability, and sufficient wind shear. Wind shear was further maximized in the vicinity of the warm front, resulting in a localized corridor of higher tornado potential. Supercell thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and continued into the evening. These storms produced all severe hazards, but the most common hazard was large hail, the largest of which was two inches in diameter in Mason County. A brief tornado occurred in Tazewell County. Training thunderstorms resulted in a narrow corridor of heavy rain from Fulton to Tazewell County, where several reports of flooded roadways were received. Radar estimates suggested 2 to 4 inches of rain fell in these areas.
episodes.212006: During the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026,  and early spring supercell thunderstorm event spread across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. This brought several swaths of damaging wind, large hail, and several tornadoes to both Iowa and Illinois.
episodes.212144: A broken line of thunderstorms developed over Illinois in the afternoon and tracked into northern Indiana. Wind gusts of 55 mph to 65 mph were recorded resulting in at least one instance of tree and property damage.
episodes.212327: Isolated severe storms over southwest Georgia resulted in wind damage and large hail.
episodes.212430: Strong to severe thunderstorms occurred along a warm front in southern WI and produced damaging winds across southeastern WI as it pushed out over Lake Michigan.
episodes.212450: At the surface, a low wobbled eastward from southern QC to northern ME. This allowed the trailing cold front to sweep generally southeastward across northern OH and northwest PA toward southern OH and southwestern PA. Along and ahead of the front, clusters of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across interior northern OH and generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage and marginally-severe hail in Marion, Morrow, and Holmes Counties. These thunderstorms occurred in a relatively-warm and moist sector comprised of weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate effective bulk shear.
episodes.212464: Low pressure and a warm front brought a round of severe thunderstorms to southern WI during the evening. Large hail and damaging straight-line winds occurred.
episodes.212486: Strong to severe thunderstorms traversed southeast Nebraska during the afternoon hours of April 3rd, 2026. Ahead of the convective activity, a low pressure system lifted northeast over eastern Nebraska and western Iowa. An associated warm front lifted into east-central Nebraska and west-central Iowa, while a cold front trailed behind it. Within the warm sector, temperatures warmed into the 60s and 70s through the day. Thunderstorms developed along the front during the afternoon. As these storms moved through southeast Nebraska, the public reported quarter-sized hail (estimated at one inch in diameter) 3 miles northeast of Shubert, NE at 2:02 PM CST.
episodes.212655: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across south-central Kansas during the afternoon hours. These thunderstorms produce large hail near Andover.
episodes.212777: A wet pattern developed during the first days of the month as above normal moisture, a nearby upper-level trough and a weak  trade wind cap supported shower and thunderstorm development. This included frequent passing showers across windward sectors, followed by enhanced afternoon convection. Flooding and Landslide reports where received during this period, April 1st to 5th.
episodes.213043: A line of thunderstorms moved across south central and southeast Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 3rd. A few reports of hail were received.
episodes.213194: A warm and moist airmass was in place across southeast Louisiana on April 2nd, with scattered to numerous thunderstorms developing during the afternoon and evening hours. Storms became oriented north to south and repeatedly redeveloped while slowly shifting east across Tangipahoa Parish. This allowed heavy rainfall to fall over some of the same areas for an extended period. A stronger storm also produced localized wind damage near Tickfaw.
episodes.213286: Warm temperatures during early April began to melt 2-3 feet of dense snowpack that had fallen across parts of northern Michigan in the historic mid-March winter storm, including Beaver Island. Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across northern Michigan through mid-April as well, resulting in total rainfall through the month of April across northern Michigan ranging from 5 to as much as nearly 16 inches at the Wellston Tippy Dam cooperative observing site in southeastern Manistee county. Traverse City, Houghton Lake, and Gaylord all recorded their wettest Aprils on record. Coupled with thawing ground and saturated soils, this resulted in widespread historic flooding across all of the northern Lower Peninsula. 20 USGS river gauges in the region set new all-time records, most of which broke the previous records by 1-2 feet. This, too, resulted in enhanced concern for multiple high-impact dams to be overtopped, including the Cheboygan Dam in the town of Cheboygan, which reached a height of just under 6 inches from the top at its peak, and the Bellaire Dam in northwest Lower Michigan. Many inland lake levels further upstream in the Cheboygan River basin were also well above normal, resulting in damage from flooding and ice shoves as winds pushed chunks of floating ice into homes along the shores; the high groundwater content and high water levels also caused widespread impacts to public and private water supplies and wastewater treatment facilities. Multiple portions of multiple roads also failed during this period, including M-119, the Tunnel of Trees, a famous tourist route along the Lake Michigan coastline between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, and the heavily-trafficked Beitner Rd Bridge south of Traverse City on the Boardman River; the river gauge at this latter location was also swept away when the culverts and roadway failed. Portions of roads that received damage are likely to remain closed for months. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. By April 15th, Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer had declared a state of emergency for 21 counties in northern Michigan within the WFO Gaylord, MI forecast area; President Donald Trump issued a Major Disaster Declaration for these same counties on June 30th. Total flood damage estimates as of July 2026 exceeded $800 million.
episodes.213765: A surface low lifted out of Missouri and into Iowa with storms developing on the associated warm front. The instability gradient skimmed southern Iowa with near 1000 J/kg MLCAPE while mid level lapse rates were around 7 C/km. Effective bulk shear of 45 kts was enough to organize storms and maintain updrafts. While widespread severe storms did not occur with convection, largely due to better instability confined south of the area, a cell in Taylor county produced hail up to golf ball sized.
